module: M00 · Dev environment, the command line & Git
businessFraming: On real teams, an un-versioned "final_analysis_v3_ACTUAL.ipynb" folder is how a company loses a week of work, ships a number nobody can reproduce, and can't answer "who changed this and why" during an audit. The Git repo you stand up this week is the foundation every future pipeline, model, and dashboard gets committed into — reproducibility and traceability start here, not later.
labSummary: Stand up the course's foundational Git repository the way a real data team would: a Python virtual environment, one installed dependency pinned in requirements.txt, a tiny runnable script, a .gitignore that keeps secrets and the venv out of history, and a clear README. You practice the everyday DE workflow — feature branch, at least three small atomic commits, and a pull request you open, review, and merge — so the mechanics are muscle memory before any data is involved.
labSteps: Create the repo skeleton locally: make the folder tree shown in the scaffold (src/, data/raw/, data/processed/, notes/, README.md, .gitignore, requirements.txt), then run `git init` and confirm `git status` shows the untracked files.

Create and activate a virtual environment (`python -m venv .venv` then `source .venv/bin/activate`, or the Windows equivalent), install ONE package (e.g. `pip install requests`), and freeze it with `pip freeze > requirements.txt`. Verify `.venv/` is ignored by confirming it does NOT appear in `git status`.

Write the small script `src/check_env.py` from the starter scaffold: complete the TODOs so it prints the Python version and confirms the installed package imports — this is your proof the environment is reproducible from requirements.txt alone.

Make your FIRST commit on `main` containing only the baseline: .gitignore, README skeleton, and requirements.txt (do not commit .venv or data files). Confirm with `git log --oneline` that exactly one commit exists.

Create and switch to a feature branch (`git switch -c feature/env-setup`), then build up the work in at least THREE atomic commits — e.g. (a) add `src/check_env.py`, (b) fill in the README run instructions, (c) add a `notes/decisions.md` entry. Each commit message states WHAT changed and WHY in the imperative mood.

Push the branch to GitHub (`git push -u origin feature/env-setup`) and open a Pull Request whose description explains what the repo is for and lists the acceptance items as a checklist a reviewer can tick off.

Self-review the PR diff in the GitHub UI as if you were a teammate: confirm no secrets, no .venv, and no large data files leaked into the diff; leave at least one review comment on your own PR, then merge it (squash or merge-commit, chosen deliberately) and delete the branch.

Prove idempotency of your setup: on a clean checkout (or after `git switch main && git pull`), recreate the venv from scratch and run `pip install -r requirements.txt` followed by `python src/check_env.py` — it must succeed with no manual fixes. Record this in `notes/decisions.md`.

Write a 4-6 line `notes/decisions.md` reflection: which files you deliberately kept OUT of Git and why, why you chose squash vs merge-commit, and what a teammate would need to reproduce your environment.

module: M01 · The DE mental model & the data lifecycle
businessFraming: NYC agencies dispatch crews (potholes, downed trees, heat/hot-water complaints) off dashboards fed by 311. When a complaint type is quietly renamed or a request lands with a null borough/lat-long, those rows drop out of the filtered view and the crew never gets routed — the outage is invisible because the dashboard still renders. A stated grain and a one-page data contract are the cheapest insurance against that silent failure.
labSummary: Pull a live sample of NYC 311 Service Requests from the Socrata API, inspect the real mess (drifting complaint types, null locations, late-closed tickets), then map the record's end-to-end lifecycle as a Mermaid diagram and write a one-page data contract that declares the grain, the required fields, the known failure modes, and the downstream consumers who break when the data drifts. Deliverable is documentation, not a pipeline — but every claim in it must be backed by something you actually observed in the sample.
labSteps: Land the data: run the provided curl scaffold to pull ~50 live rows from https://data.cityofnewyork.us/resource/erm2-nwe9.json into sample_311.json, then open it and skim the raw JSON so you see the actual field names (e.g. unique_key, complaint_type, descriptor, borough, latitude, incident_zip, created_date, closed_date, status).

Profile the mess concretely: for your sample, count how many rows have a null borough, latitude, or incident_zip; list the distinct complaint_type values; and find at least one record that is 'closed' but has no closed_date (or a closed_date before created_date). Record the exact counts and one example unique_key for each problem — these become your evidence.

Identify the grain in one sentence: state what exactly one row represents (one service request identified by unique_key) and name the column that makes it unique. Verify it by checking that unique_key has no duplicates in your sample; note what you'd do if it did.

Map the lifecycle: starting from the Mermaid skeleton, draw the record's journey from citizen intake (call/app/web) through the 311 system, the Socrata/Open Data publication layer, ingestion, storage, and the two or three dashboards/consumers at the end. On the edges where the data can silently break, annotate the failure (e.g. 'complaint_type renamed upstream', 'null borough -> dropped by borough filter', 'late closed_date -> SLA metric wrong').

Write the one-page data contract (Markdown) with these sections: Grain; Source & refresh cadence; Required (non-null) fields and their types; Known failure modes with the evidence counts from step 2; Idempotency/rerun policy (state how a re-pull must not create duplicate rows — merge on unique_key); and Consumers (who reads it and what breaks for them when a field drifts or goes null).

Declare consumers explicitly: name at least two downstream consumers (e.g. 'crew-routing dashboard filters on borough + complaint_type', 'SLA report aggregates closed_date - created_date') and, for each, write the one sentence describing the concrete harm when the contract is violated.

Write a short 'why' note (3-5 sentences): defend one real decision you made — for example, why you chose unique_key as the merge key for idempotent reloads, or why you treat null borough as a quarantine-worthy reject rather than a silent drop. This note is your interview answer.

Assemble README.md containing the business framing, the embedded Mermaid diagram, the data contract, the consumer list, and the why-note; commit sample_311.json alongside it as the evidence the numbers came from.

module: M02 — Python I: control flow & functions
businessFraming: Ops and monitoring teams live or die by threshold alerting on live feeds: page someone at M5.0, stay quiet at M2.0. If a single blank or malformed record crashes the alerting job, the whole feed goes dark and a real event slips past unnoticed — a trust and safety failure. This week you build that alerting loop against a real seismic feed that changes every minute and ships dirty rows.
labSummary: Build quakestats.py, a command-line tool that reads the live USGS all_day earthquake CSV, filters events above a magnitude threshold passed on the command line, and prints a summary — while surviving blank/missing magnitudes and malformed place strings instead of crashing. You will structure the logic into parse, classify, and summarize functions and prove robustness by running it twice with different thresholds.
labSteps: Fetch a snapshot: download the all_day CSV once to a local file (e.g. `curl -sL https://earthquake.usgs.gov/earthquakes/feed/v1.0/summary/all_day.csv -o all_day.csv`) so you develop against a stable copy, then open it and note the columns (time, latitude, longitude, depth, mag, place, ...) and confirm some `mag` fields are blank.

Parse argv: read the magnitude threshold from sys.argv[1], convert it to float, and exit with a clear usage message and non-zero status if it is missing or non-numeric (fail loud on operator error, not silently).

Write parse_row(row): given a csv.DictReader row, return a clean dict with a float magnitude and a safe place string — but when `mag` is blank or non-numeric, do NOT default it to 0.0; instead flag the row as unparseable and return it (or None) so the caller can quarantine it. Handle malformed/missing place with a fallback like 'unknown location'.

Quarantine bad records: collect every row that fails magnitude parsing into a rejected list with the reason (e.g. 'blank mag', 'non-numeric mag') and the event id, and write them to rejected.csv with a reason column — never let a bad row silently vanish or crash the loop.

Write classify(mag): using if/elif/else control flow, bucket a magnitude into a severity label (e.g. minor < 3.0, light 3.0–4.9, moderate 5.0–5.9, strong 6.0+); write summarize(events) to count how many valid events cleared the threshold, group counts by severity, and track the single strongest quake and its place.

Loop and filter: iterate the CSV with csv.DictReader, call parse_row on each, skip+quarantine failures, keep only events with mag >= threshold, and feed survivors to classify/summarize. Print a readable report: total rows read, count above threshold, counts per severity, the strongest event, and how many rows were rejected and why.

Run it twice against the same snapshot with different thresholds (e.g. `python quakestats.py 2.0` then `python quakestats.py 4.5`) and confirm the above-threshold count drops while the rejected count stays identical — the dirty-data handling is threshold-independent.

Write a 4–6 sentence NOTES.md: state exactly what you did with blank magnitudes and why (quarantine vs. drop vs. default-to-zero — and why defaulting to 0.0 would silently hide real events), and note that re-running overwrites rejected.csv rather than appending, so reruns stay idempotent.

4. Diagnose why it is slow: identify that the Seq Scan reads every row and that to_date(obs_date,'YYYYMMDD') in the WHERE clause is non-sargable, so no index on the date could even be used. Write down the bottleneck operator and the reason in your decision note.

Add ONE index that serves the filter + aggregation (compose station_id, element, and the sargable date column; consider column order and whether an index-only scan is achievable by INCLUDE-ing value). Run ANALYZE, re-EXPLAIN, and confirm the plan switched to an Index/Index-Only Scan with fewer buffers.

8. Write the decision note (tuning.md): the operator you fixed, the predicate rewrite, the index you added and its column order rationale, and — critically — one index you deliberately did NOT add (e.g. a single-column index on element with tiny cardinality, or a redundant index the planner would ignore) and why.

businessFraming: NYC's restaurant-inspection feed repeats a venue's name, address, borough, and cuisine on every single inspection and violation row — so when a restaurant changes its name or moves, you either update dozens of rows correctly or silently corrupt your data, and a brand-new venue with no inspection yet can't even be recorded. Those are the exact update, delete, and insert anomalies that normalization exists to kill, and getting them wrong is how a public health dashboard shows a shuttered address as "grade pending."

Split the flat file into the normalized tables idempotently, then PROVE integrity by watching DuckDB reject an FK-violating insert and a duplicate-PK insert, add one deliberately justified denormalization, and ship the whole thing as your Phase 1 capstone README.

DISCOVER KEYS & ANOMALIES: verify candidate keys empirically — test whether camis alone, (camis, inspection_date, inspection_type), and (camis, inspection_date, inspection_type, violation_code) are unique; write down which grain each represents (restaurant vs inspection vs violation) and note the nulls in violation_code/grade/inspection_date that break naive keys.

SELECT DISTINCT statements (lookups first, then restaurant, inspection, violation) to populate the normalized tables; make reruns safe by using CREATE OR REPLACE / DELETE-before-load / anti-join so a second run produces zero duplicate rows — state which idempotency strategy you chose and why.
